title: One person, two natures
hook: Chalcedon: without confusion, change, division or separation

segments.voice: Yesterday, why God became human: Athanasius said to draw us into God's life, Anselm said to pay what we owed. Your line was he became what we are. When did you notice your own tiredness or hunger? Day one thousand eighty-one.

A boat in a storm on the Sea of Galilee. Waves coming over the side. The disciples bailing, shouting. And in the back of the boat, Mark's Gospel says, Jesus is "asleep on a pillow." Worn out, like any man after a long day. They shake him awake. Then, in the King James, "he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still." And the sea goes flat. One minute, a tired man asleep on a cushion. The next, a voice the wind obeys. Same boat, same person. How do you say who that is, without dropping one half? Today's word: one person.

The Gospels keep doing this. On the way to the tomb of his friend Lazarus, John's Gospel has two words: "Jesus wept." A few lines later the same Jesus stands at the grave and cries, "Lazarus, come forth." Grief, and then a voice that calls the dead. Christians searched for words that keep both. At the council of Chalcedon, bishops said Christ is one person in two natures, truly God and truly human. And they added four guard rails, each a without. Without confusion: the two aren't blended into some third thing. Without change: neither turns into the other. Without division, and without separation: there aren't two people in the boat, one sleeping and one commanding. It's one who. One person. That's the word. One of the council's Greek words for person was hypostasis: the who, the one acting in everything he does. So it is the same one who weeps and who calls Lazarus out. The same one who sleeps and who stills the sea. Christians read these scenes with both hands. Not a man who was only very holy. Not God wearing a human costume. Both, not either. Not every church accepted Chalcedon's exact wording; some ancient churches of the east prefer to speak of one united nature, and they too confess him fully God and fully human. Day seven hundred eighty-three told that story. Today the point is the shape of the answer. It doesn't solve the mystery. It refuses to drop either half of it.

Here's the practice: hold two truths at once. Settle, and breathe. Rest one hand, palm up, on each knee. In your left hand, put something true about your life that's hard. In your right, something true that's good. Don't let either one cancel the other. Don't rush to decide which one is really true. Both are. Feel the two hands, the two weights, and one breath going in and out between them. If you pray, you can hold the line from Mark: Peace, be still. If you don't, just keep both hands open until the bell. The bell holds the time.
One person. Chalcedon's answer: Christ is one person, truly God and truly human, two natures without confusion, change, division or separation.
Your line: both, not either. Today, when you catch yourself saying it's either this or that, stop and ask whether it might be both. Day one thousand eighty-one.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches that hold the early creeds accept Chalcedon's definition of Christ as one person in two natures, while the Oriental Orthodox churches speak of one united nature; all of them confess him truly God and truly human.

notes: The 'shortest verse' claim about John 11:35 was cut under the claims rule; the script says only that the verse has two words. No date for Chalcedon given.

The Chalcedonian Definition is paraphrased (four adverbs: asynchytos, atreptos, adiairetos, achoristos). Schaff's Creeds of Christendom has a public-domain translation ('inconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably'); quote only after confirming exact wording.

The Oriental Orthodox are mentioned briefly and fairly, with a pointer to day 783 (Chalcedon); confirm. howItsDone says Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches that hold the early creeds accept the definition; confirm.
Avoided the 'paint mixing' picture used on day 301 and the 'fences' picture of day 783; this day uses the storm (Mark 4) and Lazarus (John 11).
Original: ὑπόστασις, glossed only as 'person' (no etymology given). The teach calls it 'the who, the one acting in everything he does'; confirm the gloss and stress (hoo-POH-sta-sis).

Editor: the Definition pairs prosopon with hypostasis, so 'the word for person' became 'one of the council's Greek words for person'. The storm story was checked against day 1067, whose practice no longer uses it.
Auditor: John 11:35 ('Jesus wept') comes before Jesus reaches the tomb (11:38); 'at the tomb' changed to 'on the way to the tomb' in the teach and the myth.
